name: Ivan Lendl

techniqueNotes.note: Strong eastern grip with a distinctive elbow-led takeback, then a fast, heavy topspin swing with contact well in front and a full finish across the body. He ran around backhands to hit it inside-out, the prototype of the modern power-baseline pattern.

Developed a topspin one-hander to add to his slice: full shoulder turn, racquet dropped below the ball, and an upward drive with the arm extending out through contact so he could pass down the line under pressure.
A very high, consistent toss and a meticulous identical pre-serve routine on every point; the routine is as copyable as the motion because it stabilises rhythm under pressure.

lesson: Build a forehand you can dictate with, then use fitness and footwork to hit it from anywhere.

name: John McEnroe

techniqueNotes.note: Started almost side-on to the baseline with his back half-turned to the opponent, creating extreme shoulder coil that unwound into a swinging lefty slice. The closed stance hid the direction and pulled right-handers far wide in the ad court.

One continental grip for every shot and extremely soft hands: he met the ball in front with almost no backswing and absorbed pace by relaxing the grip at contact, guiding drop and angle volleys rather than punching them.
Very short takeback with the ball taken on the rise, redirecting the opponent's pace with a continental grip. Copy the early contact and compact swing; most learners should use a more modern grip.

lesson: Soft hands and early contact beat big swings: touch is a skill you can train.

name: Mats Wilander

techniqueNotes.note: Compact, very repeatable two-hander with an early unit turn, a modest loop and topspin generated by the legs lifting through contact. He hit it with high net clearance crosscourt and changed direction down the line only on balanced balls.

Added a one-handed slice backhand mid-career: release the top hand, continental grip, carve high-to-low and stay sideways. It gave him a change of pace, a low approach shot and better defence when stretched.
Shot selection was his weapon: crosscourt with margin when neutral or defending, attack only off short balls, and come to the net selectively behind deep approaches.

lesson: Percentage shot selection and one added shot (the slice) can lift a solid game to the very top.

name: Boris Becker

techniqueNotes.note: Rocked his weight back then forward in a pronounced rhythm, with a very deep knee bend and a grip shifted slightly toward eastern backhand for a heavy ball. He exploded upward and into the court, landing well inside the baseline already moving to the net.
Famous for the diving volley, but the teachable part is the intent: he committed fully with a big final lunge step and kept the racquet face firm and in front, even at full stretch.
Stood in and took big cuts at second serves, especially with a blocked or driven backhand return struck early with a short backswing and his weight moving forward.

lesson: Use your legs on the serve: deep knee bend, drive up and land inside the court.

name: Stefan Edberg

techniqueNotes.note: Preferred a heavy kick serve over pace: toss slightly behind and to the left of the head, arch the back, and brush up and across the ball. The slower, high-bouncing delivery bought him time to get an extra step closer to the net for the first volley.

Textbook technique: continental grip, split step as the opponent hits, shoulder turn instead of a backswing, contact out in front with the racquet head above the wrist, and a step through the ball. His backhand volley was hit with underspin and kept deep and low.
Elegant one-hander with a full shoulder turn, the front shoulder pointing at the ball, and the arm straightening through contact out in front while the back arm extends behind for balance.

lesson: A spin serve plus a disciplined split step gets you to the net in position to volley well.

name: Yannick Noah

techniqueNotes.note: Big kick and flat serves hit with a powerful leg drive; he served and volleyed even on clay, using the high-bouncing kick serve to push returners back and give himself time to close.
Outstanding leaping overhead: turned sideways, pushed off the back foot and used a scissor kick to hit lobs at full height, which let him crowd the net without fear of being lobbed.
Chipped the backhand low and came in behind it rather than rallying, keeping the slice deep and using his athleticism to cover the pass.

lesson: An attacking net game can work on any surface if your approach shots are deep and your overhead is reliable.

name: Pat Cash

techniqueNotes.note: Stayed very low on the first volley with a deep knee bend, back straight and racquet head up, punching through the ball with a short stroke. On low volleys he bent the knees instead of dropping the racquet head.
Sprinted in behind the serve, made a balanced split step as the returner swung, then pushed off explosively in the direction of the return, always moving forward through the volley.
Served for placement and net position, mixing body serves and wide sliders so the return came back where his first volley was waiting.

lesson: Get low with your legs on the volley and keep moving forward through contact.

name: Miloslav Mečíř

techniqueNotes.note: Held the racquet back until the last moment with identical preparation for crosscourt and down-the-line, changing direction only with late hand and hip timing. The disguise wrong-footed opponents more than pace did.
Called the Big Cat for deceptively smooth, economical movement: he read the ball early and glided into position with few wasted steps, arriving balanced and unhurried.
Relaxed, flat eastern forehand that absorbed and redirected the opponent's pace, using angles and changes of speed rather than heavy topspin.

lesson: Disguise and placement, hit from identical preparation, can beat power.

name: Johan Kriek

techniqueNotes.note: One of the quickest players of his era; an explosive first step and low, sprinter-like posture let a relatively small player attack and defend on fast grass.
Returned aggressively on grass with a short backswing, taking the ball early and low and chipping or driving it at the feet of the incoming server.
Attacked the net behind serve and approach with fast hands, keeping volleys compact and relying on speed to close the distance.

lesson: Speed and a compact return let a smaller player take on the big servers.

name: Henri Leconte

techniqueNotes.note: Explosive lefty forehand hit with a very fast arm and wrist release, taken early and on the rise to create sharp angles; spectacular but high-risk because of its low margin.
Lefty slice serve swung wide in the ad court, tossed slightly further out to the side to carve around the ball, then followed to the net to volley into the open court.
Instinctive touch volleys and half-volleys played with a loose grip and open face, including stop volleys that died near the net.

lesson: Flair works best when paired with margin: take the ball early, but pick your moments.

name: Martina Navratilova

techniqueNotes.note: Lefty slice serve swung wide to the right-hander's backhand in the ad court, hit with a continental grip and a toss slightly to her left. She landed inside the baseline and was split-stepping near the service line before the return was struck.

Closed very tight to the net and volleyed with a firm wrist, short punch and forward body movement, angling the first volley away and finishing the second. Her positioning followed the ball, shading toward the line of the likely pass.
Chip-and-charge backhand: continental grip, short high-to-low carve, contact in front while already moving forward, keeping the ball low so the opponent had to hit the pass upward.

lesson: Every approach and serve should be hit with your feet already carrying you to the net.

name: Hana Mandlíková

techniqueNotes.note: Could hit the one-hander with topspin, flat or slice from the same fluid preparation: a full shoulder turn, a loose arm and a free release through contact that produced sudden winners down the line.
A natural athlete at net with quick reflexes, taking volleys early and well in front and mixing deep punches with soft angled touch.
Graceful, light movement that let her switch from baseline rally to net attack within a single point, approaching on any short ball.

lesson: Learn every spin on the backhand from one preparation so you can attack or defend at will.

name: Tracy Austin

techniqueNotes.note: Compact two-hander with early preparation and a flat-to-slight-topspin swing, struck on the rise from close to the baseline with both arms extending through contact toward the target.
Simple, repeatable eastern forehand with a short backswing and a long follow-through, aimed deep and close to the lines with relentless accuracy rather than power.
Won by making almost no unforced errors and hitting every ball deep, moving opponents side to side until the error came; her concentration point after point was the real weapon.

lesson: Depth and accuracy from compact strokes will beat more powerful but erratic opponents.

name: Pam Shriver

techniqueNotes.note: At six feet tall she used her reach to cover the net, volleying with a continental grip, a firm wrist and minimal backswing; her net positioning made her one of the great doubles players.
Sliced both the backhand and often the forehand, using a chopped continental-grip stroke to keep the ball low and approach behind it rather than trade topspin from the baseline.
Served with good variety and placement and followed it in on all surfaces, relying on a solid first volley rather than aces.

lesson: Low slices and smart net positioning make a serve-and-volley game work without big groundstrokes.

name: Andrea Jaeger

techniqueNotes.note: Steady two-handed backhand hit with early shoulder turn and a compact swing, kept deep crosscourt with good net clearance and rarely missed.
Quick court coverage and early positioning let her retrieve and reset points, recovering behind the baseline centre after each shot.
Countered serve-and-volleyers with well-disguised lobs and dipping passing shots hit from the same two-handed preparation.

lesson: Consistency and court coverage from the baseline can neutralise a net rusher.

name: Helena Suková

techniqueNotes.note: At 6 ft 2 in she hit down on the serve from a high contact point with full arm extension, producing steep angles and a high-bouncing delivery she followed to the net.
Long reach and a firm, simple punch volley; she took one big crossover step to cut off passes and kept the racquet out in front of her body.
Her height made the overhead a reliable finishing shot: early sideways turn, free arm up to track the ball, and contact at full stretch.

lesson: Contact the serve at full extension: every centimetre of height improves your angles.

name: Zina Garrison

techniqueNotes.note: Very fast and agile, she chipped and charged on returns and covered the net with quick lateral steps and a well-timed split step.
Reflex volleys hit with a compact motion and the racquet kept in front, often angled sharply crosscourt to finish points quickly.
Sliced backhand approach kept low and deep with a continental grip, hit while moving forward so she arrived at the net balanced.

lesson: Attack second serves with a chip return and follow it in to pressure the server.

name: Claudia Kohde-Kilsch

techniqueNotes.note: A tall player (about 6 ft 1 in) with a strong first serve hit from a high contact point, used to set up a forehand or a net approach on the next ball.
Flat, powerful eastern forehand hit with a long swing and forward weight transfer, used as an approach shot to come in behind.
Reach and doubles experience made her solid at net: simple punch volleys directed deep, with her long stride closing the net quickly.

lesson: Use a big serve to earn a short ball, then move forward behind your forehand.

name: Manuela Maleeva

techniqueNotes.note: Reliable two-hander with early racquet preparation and a smooth, level swing, directed deep crosscourt with margin and changed down the line only on comfortable balls.
Positioned herself early with small adjustment steps and hit from a balanced base, which kept her error rate very low in long rallies.
Steady eastern forehand played with moderate topspin and consistent depth, building points patiently rather than forcing winners.

lesson: Balanced positioning before every shot is the root of consistency.

name: Sylvia Hanika

techniqueNotes.note: Heavy lefty topspin forehand, unusual in the women's game of the time, hit with a low-to-high swing and strong leg drive; crosscourt it kicked high to a right-hander's backhand.
Used the lefty angle, sliding the serve wide in the ad court to drag opponents off the court and open space for the next forehand.
One-handed backhand used mainly to keep the rally neutral, hit with slice or moderate topspin until she could run around to the forehand.

lesson: Heavy topspin aimed high to the opponent's backhand is a simple, repeatable winning pattern.
